title: Chapter 4.  Constitutional Status - From Union Territory to National Capital Territory

blocks.content: This is the single most exam-critical chapter for Delhi. Delhi's constitutional journey - Part C State to UT to the unique 'National Capital Territory' created by the 69th Amendment - and the recurring Lieutenant Governor-versus-Chief Minister power struggle are near-certain to appear in any exam covering this UT, especially given the major Supreme Court judgments and Parliamentary amendments of 2018-2023.
From 'Part C State' to Union Territory

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Delhi transitioned from a Part C State to a Union Territory under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
The 69th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1991 introduced Article 239AA, bestowing special constitutional status and creating the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi.
Article 239AA established a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers for Delhi to legislate on State and Concurrent List items.
The Legislative Assembly of Delhi is barred from enacting laws on three State List subjects: Public Order (Entry 1), Police (Entry 2), and Land (Entry 18).
Supreme Court rulings have affirmed that the Lieutenant Governor is generally bound by the 'aid and advice' of the elected Council of Ministers, except on reserved matters and statutory exemptions.

blocks.content: At Independence, Delhi was administered as a 'Part C State' under the original Constitution, with a Chief Commissioner as administrative head and, briefly (1952-1956), an elected Legislative Assembly and Chief Minister (the first being Chaudhary Brahm Prakash) under the Government of Part C States Act, 1951.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 abolished this arrangement, converting Delhi into a Union Territory administered directly by the Central Government through a Lieutenant Governor / Administrator, with the Legislative Assembly and the post of Chief Minister ABOLISHED for nearly four decades (1956-1991) - a fact often missed by candidates who assume Delhi always had an elected government.

During this Assembly-less period, a nominated Metropolitan Council (from 1966, under the Delhi Administration Act, 1966) provided limited advisory/deliberative functions but held no real legislative power.

★ EXAM POINT: Delhi had NO Chief Minister and NO Legislative Assembly for roughly 35 years, from 1956 to 1991 - a frequently tested historical gap that surprises many candidates who assume continuous elected government since Independence.
The 69th Constitutional Amendment (1991) & Creation of the NCT

The Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991 (which inserted Articles 239AA and 239AB into the Constitution) created the unique status of 'National Capital Territory of Delhi' (NCTD), restoring an elected Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers headed by a Chief Minister, effective from 1 February 1992 under the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 (GNCTD Act).

Article 239AA gives Delhi a special hybrid status: it has an elected Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers like a state, BUT remains constitutionally a Union Territory (not a full state), with the Lieutenant Governor retaining significant powers and certain subjects (notably 'Public Order', 'Police', and 'Land' - the so-called 'three excluded subjects', part of Entries 1, 2 and 18 of the State List) kept OUTSIDE the Delhi Assembly's legislative competence and under direct Central Government control.

This dual/hybrid arrangement - part-state, part-UT - is the single most distinctive constitutional feature of Delhi among all Indian states and Union Territories, and is the root of the recurring LG-versus-elected-government tussles covered below.

cells: Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD) Act, 1991
7 (all unreserved as of the most recent delimitation)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir are the three Union Territories with a Legislative Assembly and Chief Minister; among no-assembly UTs are Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Ladakh, DNH&DD, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands - a frequently tested comparative polity list.
The LG-Government Power Struggle: Key Supreme Court Judgments

rows: Administered directly or via Parliamentary Act
Elected Legislative Assembly with constitutional powers
Explicitly excludes Public Order, Police, and Land
Bound by 'aid and advice' of Council of Ministers on transferred subjects

blocks.content: The precise division of power between Delhi's elected government and the Lieutenant Governor has been repeatedly litigated, producing two landmark Supreme Court Constitution Bench judgments that are essential exam material.

In its 2018 judgment (Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India), a 5-judge Constitution Bench held that the LG is bound by the 'aid and advice' of the Council of Ministers on matters within the Assembly's legislative competence (i.e., excluding the three reserved subjects), and cannot act as an independent decision-making authority obstructing the elected government on those matters.

A specific dispute then arose over control of 'Services' (transfers and postings of administrative officers) - not explicitly listed among the three excluded subjects. In its May 2023 judgment, a 5-judge Constitution Bench ruled that control over Services (excluding matters connected to Public Order, Police and Land) vests with the Delhi government, not the LG/Centre.

Within days of this 2023 verdict, the Central Government promulgated an Ordinance (later enacted as the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023) creating a National Capital Civil Service Authority - chaired by the Chief Minister but comprising the Chief Secretary and a Principal Home Secretary (both effectively Centre-appointed officials) - to decide transfers/postings by majority vote, and giving the LG the final say in case of disagreement, substantially reversing the practical effect of the Court's Services verdict through ordinary legislation.

This sequence - a Supreme Court ruling in the elected government's favour, promptly followed by Parliamentary legislation restoring greater LG control - is one of the most important and frequently tested current-affairs-cum-polity narratives about Delhi's governance.

cells: LG bound by 'aid and advice' of Council of Ministers on matters within Assembly's competence
GNCTD v. Union of India (Services case, Constitution Bench)
Control over 'Services' (transfers/postings) held to vest with the Delhi government, not the LG
Created the National Capital Civil Service Authority; effectively restored greater LG/Centre control over Services
Formally enacted the Ordinance's provisions into permanent law

items: Article 239AA and Article 239AB were both added to the Constitution by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991.
Remember the three reserved subjects outside the Delhi Assembly's purview: Public Order, Police, and Land.
Under Article 239AB, the President can suspend the operation of Article 239AA during a failure of constitutional machinery in the NCT of Delhi.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: This LG-vs-CM Services dispute is Delhi's single most important and current polity topic - remember the sequence: 2018 SC ruling (limits LG power) -> 2023 SC ruling (Services to Delhi govt) -> 2023 Ordinance/Act (restores LG-weighted control via the National Capital Civil Service Authority).
The Statehood Demand

items: A long-running political demand for full statehood for Delhi (removing the 'three excluded subjects' restriction entirely) has been a recurring theme since even before 1991, championed at various points by multiple parties, most vocally by the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government (2015-2025).

Proponents argue that Delhi's large population, economy and administrative complexity justify full state powers over police and land, similar to any other Indian state; opponents cite Delhi's unique status as the seat of the Union Government and the practical/security necessity of central control over these subjects in the national capital.

As of the most recent developments, Delhi remains a 'special category' NCT rather than a full state - candidates should note this is a live, unresolved political-constitutional debate rather than a settled historical fact.

blocks.content: Quick Revision Points

items: Delhi was a 'Part C State' (1950-56) with a brief elected Assembly (1952-56, first CM Chaudhary Brahm Prakash); became a plain UT (1956-91) with NO Assembly/CM for ~35 years.
69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991 (Article 239AA) created the NCT of Delhi, effective 1 Feb 1992, restoring the Assembly and CM post.
'Three excluded subjects' outside Delhi Assembly's power: Public Order, Police, Land.
2018 SC verdict: LG bound by 'aid and advice' of Council of Ministers (except the 3 excluded subjects).

May 2023 SC verdict: Services control vests with Delhi govt -> swiftly followed by the GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023, creating the National Capital Civil Service Authority and restoring greater LG-weighted control.
Delhi, Puducherry, J&K = the only 3 UTs with a Legislative Assembly + CM.
